Pearly lanternfish (Myctophum nitidulum) exhibits a maximum standard length of 8.3 cm [Li = 8.3 cm], a measurement recorded from extensive midwater trawl surveys across the species' range in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, placing it among medium-sized myctophids. This ultimate size is attained after a prolonged somatic growth phase, reflecting the energetic constraints placed on a vertically migrating mesopelagic forager. At the onset of gonadal recrudescence, individuals measure approximately 6 cm [Lp = approximately 6 cm] in standard length, marking the transition from juvenile to potentially reproductively active life stages. The wet weight at this pubertal milestone reaches 33.1 grams [Wwp = 33.1 grams], representing a substantial investment in body mass before the allocation of resources toward gamete production begins. Field studies conducted in the eastern tropical Pacific have provided the most extensive morphological dataset for this species, confirming that the transition to maturity occurs at a relatively consistent size across populations.

Hatchlings emerge from their pelagic, yolk-laden eggs at a remarkably diminutive size, with the wet weight at birth calculated at 0.000014 grams [Wwb = calculated at 0.000014 grams]. This estimate is derived from a documented egg diameter of 0.03 cm for the closely related congener Lampanyctus ritteri, following the standard geometric relationship for spherical teleost eggs. The lecithotrophic larvae rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the initial days of development, absorbing nutrients from their yolk sac before the point-of-no-return that necessitated the onset of exogenous feeding. The larval phase is characterized by rapid growth through the preflexion and flexion stages, leading toward the metamorphic climax that coincides with settlement into a more pronounced vertical migration behavior. The substantial ratio between this minute birth mass and the maximum adult mass underscores the extreme ontogenetic trajectory typical of many lanternfish.

The species exhibits a maximum wet weight of 201 grams [Wwi = 201 grams] among the largest documented adults, a value derived from length-weight allometry applied to the pubertal length recorded in field-caught specimens. This ultimate body mass is attained over several years of continuous foraging in the deep scattering layer, where Myctophum nitidulum plays a critical trophic role as both a consumer of zooplankton and a prey item for larger pelagic predators, including tuna and cephalopods. The allometric relationship, which incorporates a species-specific condition factor for the genus, indicates that mass accumulation slows considerably after the pubertal transition, with most energy being redirected toward reproductive investment. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this asymptotic mass is relatively moderate for the genus, reflecting the species' preference for cooler, deeper waters.

Within the cold, stable waters of its typical habitat at a temperature of 6.2 °C [T = 6.2 °C], the species demonstrates a maximum recorded lifespan of 9 years [am = 9 years]. This longevity is among the more extended values reported for myctophids of comparable body size and may be linked to the low metabolic costs associated with life in persistently cold, oxygen-rich mesopelagic environments. Senescence in this species is not well documented, but observed declines in body condition among the largest individuals suggest a gradual deterioration of physiological performance. The lifespan estimate aligns closely with otolith-based age determinations from populations in the North Atlantic, confirming a slow-paced life history. This generation time is consistent with the species' strategy of repeated spawning events over several seasons.

At this same thermal regime of 6.2 °C [T = 6.2 °C], females achieve a maximum reproductive output estimated at approximately 22 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 22 eggs per day] during peak spawning periods, a rate sustained over the course of the extended breeding season. This high fecundity, coupled with a protracted spawning frequency, is typical of small mesopelagic teleosts that rely on the production of large numbers of pelagic eggs to offset high larval mortality in the open ocean. The species is iteroparous, with gravid adults collected throughout much of the year across tropical and subtropical latitudes. The combination of a moderate age at first reproduction, relatively small egg size, and high fecundity per event positions Myctophum nitidulum as a classic r-selected strategist among mesopelagic fishes, yet the extended lifespan tempers this classification, allowing for multiple reproductive bouts across its nine-year life history.
